souk-okaz.name: Souk Okaz
souk-okaz.summary: A historical market in the Hejaz region of Arabia, the largest and best known annual fair of pre-Islamic times.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

roman-persian-wars.name: Roman–Persian wars
roman-persian-wars.summary: A centuries-long series of conflicts between Rome, later the Byzantine Empire, and Persia's Parthian and Sasanian empires, lasting from 54 BC to 628 AD without a decisive outcome.

khamr.name: Khamr
khamr.summary: The Arabic term for wine or alcoholic drink, forbidden under most interpretations of Islamic law, though the Hanafi school narrowly defined it as drink made only from grapes or dates.

umar.name: Umar
umar.summary: Second Rashidun caliph, ruling 634 to 644; a close companion of Muhammad whose conquests brought Persia and much of the Byzantine Empire under Muslim rule before his assassination.

abd-allah-ibn-mas-ud.name: Abdullah ibn Masud
abd-allah-ibn-mas-ud.summary: A companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, regarded by Sunni tradition as the greatest interpreter of the Quran of his time, who lived from about 594 to 653.

taif.name: Taif
taif.summary: A city in the Hejaz mountains of Saudi Arabia, visited by the Prophet Muhammad in the early 7th century and long inhabited by the Banu Thaqif tribe.

al-ubulla.name: Al-Ubulla
al-ubulla.summary: A port city at the head of the Persian Gulf near Basra, Iraq's main commercial gateway for trade with India in medieval times.

gerrha.name: Gerrha
gerrha.summary: Ancient city in Eastern Arabia on the Persian Gulf that became a major hub for trading Arabian aromatics and goods from India after Alexander the Great's conquests.

sohar.name: Sohar
sohar.summary: The capital of Oman's Al Batinah North Governorate, an ancient port on the Gulf of Oman and, by legend, the birthplace of Sinbad the Sailor.

mokha.name: Mokha
mokha.summary: A Red Sea port city in Yemen that was the principal port for Yemen's capital and, from the 16th to 19th centuries, the world's main marketplace for coffee, giving its name to 'mocha'.

kharijites.name: Kharijites
kharijites.summary: An Islamic sect that emerged in 656 to 661 among former supporters of Ali who rejected his arbitration with Mu'awiya; their rebellions against Umayyad and later Abbasid rule continued for centuries.

great-mosque-of-sanaa.name: Great Mosque of Sanaa
great-mosque-of-sanaa.summary: One of the oldest mosques in the world, said to have been founded around 633 CE in Sanaa, Yemen, built partly from materials taken from an earlier palace and church on the site.

himyar.name: Himyar
himyar.summary: A South Arabian kingdom based in the Yemeni highlands that rose to dominate most of South Arabia by the late 3rd century CE, before falling to an Aksumite invasion in the early sixth century.

ghumdan-palace.name: Ghumdan Palace
ghumdan-palace.summary: An ancient fortified palace in Sana'a, Yemen, dating back to the Kingdom of Saba; only ruins remain today, within the Old City's UNESCO World Heritage site.

kingdom-of-aksum.name: Kingdom of Aksum
kingdom-of-aksum.summary: A powerful trading kingdom in the Horn of Africa and South Arabia, founded around the 1st century, ranked among the era's four great powers, and one of the first states to adopt Christianity, in the 4th century.

al-qalis-church.name: Al-Qalis Church
al-qalis-church.summary: A Miaphysite Oriental Orthodox cathedral built in Sanaa, Yemen, between about 527 and the late 560s by Abraha, whose lavish decoration made it a pilgrimage site rivaling the Kaaba.

muhammad.name: Muhammad
muhammad.summary: The founder of Islam, born around 570 CE in Mecca, whom Muslims believe received revelations from God beginning around 610 as the final prophet.

ibn-ishaq.name: Ibn Ishaq
ibn-ishaq.summary: An 8th-century Arab historian (c. 699–767) whose collected oral traditions formed the basis of an important early biography of Muhammad.

al-azraqi.name: Al-Azraqi
al-azraqi.summary: Ninth-century historian from Mecca whose Book of Reports about Mecca describes the pre-Islamic Kaaba's design and the sacred items once kept inside it.

sheba.name: Sheba (Saba)
sheba.summary: An ancient South Arabian kingdom in what is now Yemen, existing from around 1000–800 BCE until 275 CE, home to the Sabaean people and centered on the city of Marib.

umayyad-caliphate.name: Umayyad Caliphate
umayyad-caliphate.summary: Second Islamic caliphate, ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 661 to 750 from its capital Damascus; expanded Muslim rule across the Maghreb, Iberia, Central Asia and Sindh.

al-walid-i.name: Al-Walid I
al-walid-i.summary: Sixth Umayyad caliph (705–715) who expanded the caliphate to its largest extent and built major mosques including the Great Mosque of Damascus.

abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

qarmatians.name: Qarmatians
qarmatians.summary: An Isma'ili Shia militant movement centred in eastern Arabia from 899 CE, notorious for sacking Mecca in 930 CE and stealing the Black Stone.

sasanian-empire.name: Sasanian Empire
sasanian-empire.summary: An Iranian empire ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD, founded by Ardashir I to revive the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire; at its height it stretched from Egypt to Central Asia.

dhu-nuwas.name: Dhu Nuwas
dhu-nuwas.summary: A Jewish king of Himyar who reigned around 522 to 530 CE, remembered for persecuting the Christian community of Najran.

najran.name: Najran
najran.summary: A city in southwestern Saudi Arabia, an ancient trade and agricultural center on caravan routes, notable for its pre-Islamic Christian community.

khosrow-i.name: Khosrow I
khosrow-i.summary: Sasanian King of Kings of Iran from 531 to 579, known as Anushirvan ('the Immortal Soul'), who made peace with the Byzantines in 532, later fought them from 540, sacked Antioch, and captured Dara in 573.

wahrez.name: Wahrez
wahrez.summary: A Sasanian general of Daylamite origin, active in the Iberian War and later in the Aksumite-Persian wars.

ghassanids.name: Ghassanids
ghassanids.summary: Arab Christian kingdom and tribal confederation allied with the Roman Empire in the Levant, reaching its peak under Justinian I in the 6th century before falling in the early Muslim conquests.

lakhmid-kingdom.name: Lakhmids
lakhmid-kingdom.summary: An Arab kingdom, also called the Nasrid dynasty, that ruled parts of southern Mesopotamia and northeastern Arabia from the late 3rd century to 602 CE as a client state of Sasanian Persia, based at Al-Hira.

conquest-of-mecca.name: Conquest of Mecca
conquest-of-mecca.summary: Muhammad's military campaign that captured Mecca from the Quraysh in December 629 or January 630, formally ending their war.

hawazin.name: Hawazin
hawazin.summary: An Arab tribe based around Ta'if in the Hejaz, defeated by Muhammad's forces at the Battle of Hunayn in 630 AD after repeated clashes with Mecca and other tribes.

banu-thaqif.name: Banu Thaqif
banu-thaqif.summary: An Arab tribe of Ta'if that initially opposed Muhammad but converted to Islam after 630, later providing prominent governors and commanders for the early Caliphate.

battle-of-hunayn.name: Battle of Hunayn
battle-of-hunayn.summary: A battle around 630 CE in which Muhammad's forces defeated the Qays tribes after the conquest of Mecca; it is one of the few battles named in the Quran.

marib-dam.name: Marib Dam
marib-dam.summary: An ancient dam near Marib in Yemen, first built around the 8th century BCE and regarded as an engineering wonder central to the Sabaean and Himyarite kingdoms.

abu-sufyan.name: Abu Sufyan
abu-sufyan.summary: Meccan Quraysh leader and merchant (c. 560-653) who long opposed Muhammad militarily before submitting in 630; father of the first Umayyad caliph, Mu'awiya I.

battle-of-uhud.name: Battle of Uhud
battle-of-uhud.summary: A battle fought in March 625 near Medina between the early Muslims and the Quraysh of Mecca, in which archers left their post too soon, letting Meccan cavalry turn a Muslim advantage into defeat.

quraysh.name: Quraysh
quraysh.summary: An Arab tribe that controlled Mecca before Islam, into which the Prophet Muhammad was born; by the 7th century they were wealthy merchants dominating regional trade, and later opposed his preaching.

expedition-of-tabuk.name: Expedition of Tabuk
expedition-of-tabuk.summary: A military campaign led by Muhammad in October 630 CE with up to 30,000 men toward northern Arabia, prompted by fears of a Byzantine invasion; no battle occurred, but local chiefs submitted.

arethas-of-najran.name: Harith ibn Kaleb
arethas-of-najran.summary: Leader of the Christian community of Najran, killed around 523 by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas for refusing to convert, an event that drew in Byzantine and Aksumite forces.

battle-of-badr.name: Battle of Badr
battle-of-badr.summary: A battle fought on 13 March 624 CE near Badr, in which Muhammad's forces defeated the Quraysh army of Mecca led by Abu Jahl, beginning their six-year war.

nabataean-script.name: Nabataean script
nabataean-script.summary: A consonantal alphabet used to write Nabataean Aramaic and Arabic from the 2nd century BC, known from thousands of inscriptions found from Jordan to Saudi Arabia.

al-mufaddal-ad-dabbi.name: al-Mufaddal ad-Dabbi
al-mufaddal-ad-dabbi.summary: An 8th-century Arabic philologist of the Kufan school (died c. 780-787) who compiled an early anthology of pre-Islamic Arabic poetry, decades before Abu Tammam's Hamasah and before the scholars Abu 'Ubaidah and al-Asma'i, though a contemporary of other famous collectors of the tradition like Hammad ar-Rawiya.

mufaddaliyat.name: Mufaddaliyat
mufaddaliyat.summary: An anthology of 126 pre-Islamic Arabic poems compiled between 762 and 784 CE by Mufaddal al-Dabbi, one of five canonical sources for early Arabic poetry.

asma-iyyat.name: Asma'iyyat
asma-iyyat.summary: An early anthology of Arabic poetry compiled by al-Asma'i, containing 92 poems by 71 poets and ranked among the primary sources for pre-Islamic Arabic poetry.

al-asma-i.name: Al-Asma'i
al-asma-i.summary: Arab philologist (c. 740-828/833) and leading grammarian at the Abbasid court, who compiled the poetry anthology Asma'iyyat and wrote widely on poetry, genealogy, and natural science.

hammad-ar-rawiya.name: Hammad al-Rawiya
hammad-ar-rawiya.summary: An 8th-century Iranian-born scholar based in Kufa, considered the first person to systematically collect Arabic poetry, and credited with compiling the Mu'allaqat.

adi-ibn-zayd.name: Adi ibn Zayd
adi-ibn-zayd.summary: 6th-century Arab Christian poet from an Ibadi family of al-Hirah.

al-hira.name: Al-Hira
al-hira.summary: An ancient city in Mesopotamia, capital of the Lakhmid kingdom, the major pre-Islamic Arab client kingdom of the Sasanian Empire, remembered as an urban Christian center of poetry and music.

tayma.name: Tayma
tayma.summary: A Saudi Arabian city and major oasis in Tabuk Province, on the trade route between Medina and Dumah, with a long history of habitation.

midian.name: Midian
midian.summary: A region in northwest Arabia mentioned in the Hebrew Bible and Quran, associated with the Midianites and known in Arabic as Madyan.

imru-al-qais.name: Imru' al-Qais
imru-al-qais.summary: Pre-Islamic Arabian poet from Najd, active in the late 5th and early 6th centuries and the last king of Kinda, often called the father of Arabic poetry.

hisham-ibn-al-kalbi.name: Hisham ibn al-Kalbi
hisham-ibn-al-kalbi.summary: An 8th-century Arab Muslim historian (737–819 CE) from Kufa who collected genealogies and history of the ancient Arabs, best known for his Book of Idols on pre-Islamic pagan worship.

book-of-idols.name: Book of Idols
book-of-idols.summary: An early Islamic-era work by Arab scholar Hisham ibn al-Kalbi (737–819) describing polytheistic worship in pre-Islamic Arabia, though modern historians doubt its reliability as a source.

cih-541.name: CIH 541
cih-541.summary: A 548 CE inscription commissioned by the Himyarite ruler Abraha, describing a plague and his repair of the Marib Dam, and the last known inscription naming Sheba's former ruling family.

plague-of-justinian.name: Plague of Justinian
plague-of-justinian.summary: A pandemic (541–549 AD) that struck the Mediterranean, Europe and the Near East, killing about a fifth of Constantinople's population at its height under Emperor Justinian I.

late-antique-little-ice-age.name: Late Antique Little Ice Age
late-antique-little-ice-age.summary: A Northern Hemisphere cooling period in the 6th and 7th centuries AD, triggered by major volcanic eruptions and linked to the decline of the Roman Empire.

rashidun-caliphate.name: Rashidun Caliphate
rashidun-caliphate.summary: Early Islamic state (632–661 CE) led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad's death, which rapidly expanded into the dominant power of West Asia and North Africa.

fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

ziyadid-dynasty.name: Ziyadid dynasty
ziyadid-dynasty.summary: A Muslim dynasty that ruled western Yemen from its capital Zabid from 819 to 1018, the first dynasty to hold power over the Yemeni lowlands after Islam arrived.

al-ma-mun.name: Al-Ma'mun
al-ma-mun.summary: Seventh Abbasid caliph (786-833) who promoted the translation movement and flowering of science in Baghdad, during whose reign al-Khwarizmi's algebra text was published.

kaleb-of-axum.name: Kaleb of Axum
kaleb-of-axum.summary: A king of Aksum, a kingdom in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, also known and venerated under other names including Saint Elesbaan and Ella Asbeha.

hujrids.name: Hujrids
hujrids.summary: A ruling dynasty of the Kingdom of Kinda in central Arabia from roughly the 5th to early 6th century CE, acting as client rulers of the Himyarite Kingdom while dealing diplomatically and militarily with Byzantium and Persia.

anastasius-i-dicorus.name: Anastasius I
anastasius-i-dicorus.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 491 to 518 who came to the throne at 61 and enacted lasting financial and administrative reforms that strengthened the empire for successors including Justinian I.

al-mundhir-iii-ibn-al-nu-man.name: al-Mundhir III
al-mundhir-iii-ibn-al-nu-man.summary: King of the Lakhmids, reigning from 503/505 until his death in 554.

yu-firids.name: Yu'firids
yu-firids.summary: An Islamic Himyarite dynasty that ruled the Yemeni highlands from 847 to 997, centered on Sanaa and Shibam Kawkaban.

ismailism.name: Ismailism
ismailism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, one of three alongside Twelver and Zaydi Islam, marked by its distinctive emphasis on the esoteric, hidden meaning of Islamic teaching.

abraha.name: Abraha
abraha.summary: Aksumite viceroy who seized the throne of the Kingdom of Himyar in Yemen in the 6th century CE, took grand royal titles, and briefly built an empire across much of Arabia.

al-musta-in.name: al-Musta'in
al-musta-in.summary: Abbasid caliph from 862 to 866 during the 'Anarchy at Samarra,' whose reign ended in civil war with rival caliph al-Mu'tazz and his own execution.

khutbah.name: Khutbah
khutbah.summary: The formal sermon of Islamic public preaching, delivered especially at Friday congregational prayers and on festival days, by a speaker called a khatib.

monastery-of-hind-the-elder.name: Hind
monastery-of-hind-the-elder.summary: A Hujrid princess who sponsored the building of a monastery at Al-Hira, capital of the Lakhmid kingdom; she was the wife of Lakhmid king Al-Mundhir III and daughter of al-Harith ibn Amr, the most famous king of Kinda.

jahiliyyah.name: Jahiliyyah
jahiliyyah.summary: Islamic term for the pre-Islamic 'Age of Ignorance,' traditionally portrayed as barbaric to contrast with Muhammad's mission; modern historians reject this narrative.

g-r-hawting.name: Gerald Hawting
g-r-hawting.summary: British historian, born 1944, specializing in Quranic studies and Islamic studies.

miaphysitism.name: Miaphysitism
miaphysitism.summary: A Christian doctrine holding that Jesus is fully divine and fully human in a single nature, held by the Oriental Orthodox Churches in contrast to the two-nature view set at Chalcedon in 451.

nestorianism.name: Nestorianism
nestorianism.summary: A set of Christian theological teachings on the two natures or persons of Christ, originally tied to bishop Nestorius and condemned at the Council of Ephesus.

mishnah.name: Mishnah
mishnah.summary: The first written collection of Jewish oral tradition, compiled in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE and forming the basis of the Talmud.

people-of-the-book.name: People of the Book
people-of-the-book.summary: An Islamic classification for followers of religions seen as having received divine scripture, chiefly Jews and Christians, historically taxed for religious autonomy under Muslim rule.

mary-mother-of-jesus.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
mary-mother-of-jesus.summary: First-century Jewish mother of Jesus, venerated in Christianity as Mother of God and also honored in Islam, which names a Quranic chapter after her.

jesus.name: Jesus
jesus.summary: A 1st-century Jewish preacher in Roman Judaea regarded by Christians as the Messiah and central figure of Christianity, whose life is recorded chiefly in the Gospels.

arab-states-of-the-persian-gulf.name: Khaleeji
arab-states-of-the-persian-gulf.summary: Term for the seven Arab states bordering the Persian Gulf: Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, most once British protectorates.
arab-states-of-the-persian-gulf.source_title: Arab states of the Persian Gulf

majlis.name: Majlis
majlis.summary: Arabic word meaning 'sitting room', used for social or administrative gatherings in Muslim-influenced cultures, and also for some legislative councils.

sanaa.name: Sanaa
sanaa.summary: Capital and largest city of Yemen, at 2,300 metres in the Sarawat Mountains, with an Old City that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sabaic.name: Sabaic
sabaic.summary: An ancient South Arabian language spoken by the Sabaeans from about 1000 BC to the 6th century AD, closely related to and possibly mutually intelligible with Arabic.

gargee-an.name: Gargee'an
gargee-an.summary: A centuries-old Eastern Arabian holiday held twice during Ramadan and Sha'ban, when children in traditional dress go door-to-door singing for sweets.

sha-ban.name: Sha'ban
sha-ban.summary: The eighth month of the Islamic calendar, whose name means 'to disperse,' and the last lunar month before Ramadan.

wadi-al-qura.name: Wadi al-Qura
wadi-al-qura.summary: A valley north of Medina, Saudi Arabia, on the main trade road to Syria, described in early sources as fertile and full of villages, and the site of several military expeditions during Muhammad's time.

al-ula.name: Al-Ula
al-ula.summary: An ancient oasis city in northwest Arabia on the incense trade route, once capital of the Lihyanites and near the Nabataean site of Hegra.

francis-edward-peters.name: F. E. Peters
francis-edward-peters.summary: American academic (1927–2020) who was professor emeritus of history, religion, and Middle Eastern and Islamic studies at New York University.

abu-muhammad-al-hasan-al-hamdani.name: al-Hasan al-Hamdani
abu-muhammad-al-hasan-al-hamdani.summary: Arab Muslim geographer, chemist, poet, grammarian, historian and astronomer (c. 893-947) from Yemen, considered one of the finest scholars of late Abbasid Islamic culture.
